pages.d: For a decade the default was human driven, AI assisted. That order is inverting — and the part left to a person gets harder, not easier. What actually changes.
pages.b: AI Driven, Human Assisted | Krunalkumar Shah AI practice AI driven, human assisted: the default just inverted For most of the last decade the sensible arrangement was obvious — a person did the work, and a model helped at the edges. That order is flipping. The model holds the plan now and the person holds the veto, and the half left to the human turns out to be the harder half. Here is what actually changed, the four jobs that stay with you, where the inversion is a bad idea, and how I run it in production. Published 21 August 2026 · 12 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The old default, and why it worked Human driven, AI assisted was never a slogan anybody had to argue for. It was simply how the tools worked. Autocomplete finished the line you were already writing. The grammar checker flagged a sentence you had already composed. The model suggested a function body inside a file you had already structured, in a project you had already designed. You held the plan; the tool shaved seconds off the typing. That arrangement was safe for a reason worth naming out loud: the unit of delegation was small enough to check at a glance. If a suggestion was wrong, you saw it the second it appeared, in context, with everything around it still loaded in your head. The cost of a bad suggestion was one keystroke — reject, move on. Nobody ever needed a governance policy for autocomplete. It was also, quietly, a ceiling. A tool that only ever operates one line ahead of you can never save you more than the typing. The thinking, the sequencing, the twenty small decisions between "I need this" and "this works" — all of it stayed with the human, because there was no way to hand any of it over. What actually changed The popular story is that the models got smarter. That is true, and it is not the interesting part. The shift that matters is much narrower: the model started holding the sequence. Give a current system a goal instead of a sentence and it will decompose it, choose tools, run them, read what came back, notice that it was wrong, and try again — for twenty or fifty steps — before it hands you anything at all. That is a different job. It is not writing your next line. It is running the loop you used to run. And once the loop moves, the unit of delegation moves with it. You are no longer accepting a token. pages.b: Automating Email Replies with n8n | Krunalkumar Shah Automation Automating email replies with n8n Replying to the same kinds of emails over and over is exactly the sort of work software should handle. I've built several of these systems for real clients — including my open-source CleverResponder builds for SmartLead and Instantly. Here's how I structure them, where AI genuinely helps, and the mistakes worth avoiding. Published 18 May 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why n8n for this n8n is a workflow automation tool where you connect building blocks — triggers, logic, and actions — into a flow, without writing a whole application from scratch. For email reply automation it fits well for a few reasons: it talks to email and CRM services out of the box, it lets you drop in custom logic where you need it, and because you can self-host it, sensitive message content doesn't have to pass through a third-party black box. You get the speed of no-code with an escape hatch to real code when a step needs it. The anatomy of a reply-automation workflow However fancy it looks, almost every email automation I build follows the same five-stage skeleton. Understanding this shape matters more than any single node: Trigger — something starts the flow: a new reply lands in an inbox, or a campaign tool like SmartLead or Instantly fires a webhook. Fetch & parse — pull in the message and pull out what matters: sender, subject, body, and any context from a CRM about who this person is. Classify — decide what kind of message this is. Interested? Not interested? A question? Out of office? This is the single most important step, and the one people skip. Draft — generate an appropriate response, often with an AI step guided by a tight prompt and the context you gathered. Act — send the reply, or route it to a human for approval, and log the outcome back to the CRM so nothing falls through the cracks. Every reliable email automation is a variation on this: trigger, gather context, classify, draft, then act — with logging throughout. Classify before you generate The temptation with AI is to skip straight to "let the model write a reply to anything." That's how you end up sending a cheerful sales pitch to someone who wrote "please remove me from your list." The fix is to classify intent first , then let each category follow its own path. pages.b: Character Over Career: Five Choices | Krunalkumar Shah Mindset Character over career: five choices I live by Here is a small habit that runs my life. For a handful of words that start with the same letter, there are two things you could chase. Most people chase one of them. I've learned to chase the other. Same letter, different choice — and the choice makes all the difference. Published 27 July 2026 · 6 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah None of these are original virtues — you've heard all ten words before. What I find useful is the pairing: putting the two side by side forces an actual choice, and the choice reveals what you really value when both options are on the table. Here are the five I keep coming back to. The word on the left is the one I try to choose when both are within reach. Character over Career Too many people quietly trade away their moral responsibilities for a paycheck and a better title — the duty they owe their parents, their family, the people who depend on them — because a career seems to demand it. I think that trade is backwards. Character isn't the thing you sacrifice for a career; it's the thing that opens career doors in the first place. Build a reputation for being dependable, honest, and decent, and opportunities come looking for you. A career is what you have; character is who you are while you build it. Careers can be rebuilt after a setback — I've watched people recover from layoffs, failed startups, and false starts. But a reputation for how you treat people, once broken, almost never comes back. I would rather be known as someone you can trust than someone you're impressed by. The impressive fades; the trustworthy compounds. When the two ever pull in different directions, character wins, because it's the only one of the two you actually keep. Satisfaction over Success Success is measured from the outside, and the goalposts never stop moving — there is always a bigger title, a higher number, someone one rung above you. Satisfaction is measured from the inside: did the work mean something, did it help someone, would I do it again. My first paid mentoring session earned me six dollars an hour. By any definition of success, that is nothing. By the measure of satisfaction, it was everything — it told me this work was worth doing, and it pointed my whole path. pages.b: How Cybercrime Cases Are Solved | Krunalkumar Shah Security How cybercrime cases are solved: from first alert to the courtroom A breach or an online fraud starts two clocks at once — the victim's race to contain the damage, and the investigator's race to preserve the evidence. This is the full lifecycle of a cybercrime case: the incident-response track, the law-enforcement track, the digital forensics where they meet, and the courtroom where it all gets tested. Published 10 August 2026 · 14 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Two clocks start when something breaks The moment a ransomware note appears on a screen, or money leaves an account it shouldn't have, two clocks start ticking. The first is the containment clock : stop the bleeding, get systems back, keep the business alive. The second is the evidence clock : everything you will ever be able to prove about what happened is decaying — logs are rotating, RAM is volatile, and stolen money is hopping between mule accounts. These clocks pull in opposite directions, and most of the damage to a cybercrime case — as opposed to the damage from the crime itself — happens in the first few hours, before any forensic examiner or investigating officer arrives. Not through malice; through reflex. The IT team wipes the infected laptop. The embarrassed victim deletes the chat. The company "handles it quietly" and calls the police three weeks later, when the trail is stone cold. By the time an expert shows up, the case has usually already been strengthened or crippled by people who never realized they were handling evidence. This article walks the whole lifecycle: the victim's track (incident response), the law-enforcement track (complaint to charge sheet), the digital forensics where the two converge, and the admissibility rules that decide what survives in court. The legal specifics are Indian — the portal, the helpline, the statutes — but the discipline underneath is the same everywhere. Track one: the victim side of the case Incident response has a standard shape, and the one most teams borrow is the NIST lifecycle (SP 800-61): preparation , detection and analysis , containment, eradication and recovery , and post-incident activity . Real incidents loop through these phases rather than marching through them. The phase where cases are won or lost is containment — that is where the two clocks collide head-on. pages.b: How I Vibe Coded This Website | Krunalkumar Shah Engineering practice How I vibe coded this website — and the mechanism that made it hold I did not hand-write most of this site. I described what I wanted, an AI produced it, and I kept the authority over every decision that mattered. That is the easy half to explain and the wrong half to copy. What actually made it survive is the mechanism I built around the prompting — how I specify, how I verify, and what happens when something breaks. This is that mechanism, with the receipts. Published 21 August 2026 · 11 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah What vibe coding actually got me Let me be honest about the starting point, because the honesty is the useful part. I described pages in plain English and a model wrote them. The first version of this site existed in an afternoon. If you have tried it, you know the feeling — it is genuinely fast, and the output is genuinely fine. It is fine for about a week. The trouble is not that the code is bad. The trouble is that you did not build a system, you accumulated one. Nothing records why the header is structured the way it is. Nothing stops the next change from quietly contradicting the last one. You cannot answer "is this still correct?" because you never wrote down what correct meant. Ask for one more feature and you get one more layer on a foundation nobody documented, including you. This site is 96 pages now — 60 of them browser-based labs that run real language runtimes, 16 blog posts, the rest ordinary pages — across 140 commits, with zero npm dependencies. Nothing that size survives on vibes. What follows is the scaffolding that let it get there while I was still the one deciding. The prompt is a specification The single biggest change in my output quality had nothing to do with the model. It was realising that a prompt is not a wish. It is a specification, and it should be written like one. "Make the blog look nicer" is a wish. It produces something, you squint at it, you ask again. pages.b: Standing Out in an Internship Interview | Krunalkumar Shah Careers How to stand out in an internship interview Between 2021 and 2023, while working at MountBlue and consulting for US firms, I took more than 5,000 interviews. That much time on the other side of the table teaches you what actually separates candidates — and it's rarely what they spent their time preparing. Here's what actually moves the needle, from someone who has done the reviewing at scale. Published 24 June 2026 · 6 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Understand what an internship interview is really for A senior-hire interview asks "can you already do this job?" An internship interview asks a very different question: "will you be worth teaching?" Nobody expects an intern to know everything. What they are actually screening for is coachability, curiosity, and whether you finish what you start. Once you understand that shift, half of interview anxiety disappears — you stop trying to fake expertise you aren't expected to have, and start showing the traits that actually get you picked. Attitude first, aptitude second If those 5,000-plus interviews taught me one thing, it's this: I screen for attitude before aptitude. It sounds backwards — surely skill is what matters? — but the logic is simple. Aptitude can be added. I can teach a framework, a language, a tool; skills are learnable on a timeline. Attitude comes from within, and no amount of training installs it. Curiosity, honesty, the willingness to keep going when something is hard, the instinct to take ownership instead of making excuses — you either bring those to the table or you don't. So a candidate who is a little behind on skills but clearly hungry, coachable, and honest will beat a more polished one who is arrogant or passive nearly every time. What this means for you is freeing: you do not have to walk in as the finished article. You have to walk in as someone obviously worth investing in. Show the attitude, and the aptitude gap stops being disqualifying — it becomes the exact thing the internship exists to close. Do the homework almost nobody does You would be surprised how many candidates can't answer "so, what do you know about my work?" Turning up informed is rare enough that it instantly separates you. Before any interview: Read what the person or company actually does — their projects, their writing, their focus areas — and be able to name one specific thing that interested you and why . pages.b: How to Succeed in Software Development | Krunalkumar Shah Craft How to succeed in software development: the four-step path After years of building systems and reviewing thousands of engineers, I've come to trust one simple order of operations. Great software isn't written in one heroic pass — it's grown through four stages: make it work, make it modular, make it readable, then make it optimized. The magic is entirely in doing them in that order. Published 5 June 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why the order matters more than the steps Most people fail at software not because they can't do these four things, but because they do them in the wrong sequence. They optimize before it works. They polish readability on code they're about to throw away. They chase a perfectly modular architecture for a problem they don't understand yet. Each of those is effort spent in the wrong place at the wrong time. The four steps below are valuable precisely because they tell you what to care about now and what to deliberately ignore until later. Each step stands on the one before it. Skip a stair and the ones above it wobble. Step 1 — Make it work The first and only job at the start is to get something running end to end, however ugly. One long function, hard-coded values, no error handling worth mentioning — fine. The goal here is not quality; it is proof . A working-but-messy version teaches you what the problem actually is, surfaces the surprises hiding in the requirements, and gives you something real to improve. A beautiful design for the wrong problem is worthless, and you can't know the right problem until something works. The trap at this stage is perfectionism — polishing code you might delete once you understand the problem better. Resist it. Get to working first, and give yourself explicit permission for it to be rough. Step 2 — Make it modular Now that it works, you understand the problem well enough to see its natural seams. Modularity is the step where you break that one big blob into pieces that each do a single job — a function that only parses, a function that only validates, a function that only sends. Good modules have clear boundaries: you can understand one without holding all the others in your head, and you can change one without breaking its neighbors. pages.b: I Open-Sourced My AI SDR | Krunalkumar Shah Automation I open-sourced my AI SDR Of everything I've automated, this is the build I'm most proud of: CleverResponder, a fully functional AI SDR that handles campaign replies end to end — classify, draft, approve, send, follow up. I built it twice, once for SmartLead and once for Instantly, and both workflows are free on my GitHub. Here's how it works, node by node. Published 3 August 2026 · 6 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The problem: replies are where campaigns go to die Cold outreach tools are great at sending. The trouble starts when someone actually answers. Replies arrive at all hours, in every shape — "interested, send more info", "book me a call", "not interested", out-of-office bounces, and the occasional message that defies categorization. An SDR now has to read each one, figure out what it is, write a response in the company's voice, and follow up if the prospect goes quiet. Response speed matters enormously here, and it's precisely when the team is busiest that replies sit unanswered the longest. That grind is what CleverResponder removes. Not by letting an AI run wild in the inbox — by giving the boring 80% of replies a fast, safe, supervised path, so humans only touch the messages that need them. What it does, end to end Receives every campaign reply through a webhook, the moment it lands. Classifies it — interested, info requested, meeting requested, not interested, out of office, and more. Drafts a reply with AI, grounded in a knowledge document of FAQs and company details — so answers come from your facts, not the model's imagination. Asks a human — the draft lands in Slack with approve/disapprove buttons. Nothing sends without a click. Sends and follows up — approved replies go out; meeting requests get a calendar link, and if no booking happens within a few days, the workflow checks in and nudges. Here is the whole structure in one pass: what each layer says, the folklore worth unlearning, and a reference index you can bookmark. Published 10 August 2026 · Updated 17 August 2026 · 16 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The law stack nobody reads If you build or run anything digital in India, you are already inside this stack: every UPI payment, SaaS security clause, and police complaint quoting Section 66C traces back to a handful of statutes and their rules. Yet most of us meet the law only in fragments, and fragments breed folklore — misquoted sections, invented penalties, a provision struck down a decade ago still cited in complaints. I am not a lawyer — I am a security practitioner who kept meeting these laws in audits, vendor contracts, and incident calls until I read the primary texts. This is the orientation I wish someone had handed me — every claim checked against its primary source and date-stamped where the ground is moving. Not legal advice. This is practitioner orientation — a map of the terrain, not counsel about your situation. For a notice, a summons, an investigation, or a compliance decision, consult a lawyer qualified in Indian law. Verified against primary sources in August 2026; where the law is in flux, I say so. Twenty-five years of Indian IT law in one line — the timeline this article walks. The IT Act 2000: why it exists In the late 1990s India had a practical problem: contract and evidence law assumed paper. A "document" was something you could hold; a "signature" meant ink. So when the United Nations adopted the UNCITRAL Model Law on Electronic Commerce (1996) and recommended that member states legislate along its lines, India did. The Information Technology Act, 2000 came into force on 17 October 2000 — the country's first comprehensive law for electronic commerce and computer crime. A single $6 session started more than I realized at the time. Published 19 July 2026 · 9 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The classroom that didn't feel like enough I earned my bachelor's in engineering from a private state college, then a master's focused on information security. On paper that is a clean line. In reality, the classroom always felt like it was describing the world rather than letting me touch it. Lectures could tell me how a system was supposed to behave; they couldn't show me how it broke when someone poked it the wrong way. That gap — between knowing about something and having actually done it — is the thing that has shaped every decision since. So I started building and breaking things on my own machine. Most of it went nowhere. But one of those late-night rabbit holes turned into the first real milestone of my career. The paper I almost didn't write I got curious about a deceptively simple attack: the fork bomb. A tiny snippet that tells a system to endlessly copy itself until it grinds to a halt. What fascinated me was that even a properly hardened Linux machine could be brought down by it, because creating a process is a completely ordinary thing that needs no special permission. The existing defenses all had a catch — they either blocked legitimate work or punished innocent programs forever. I thought I had an idea for something better, and I nearly talked myself out of writing it up. Who was I to publish? A student. But I did the work, ran the experiments, and it became a peer-reviewed paper — Security Against Fork Bomb Attack in Linux Based Systems , published in IJRAT. It earned a silver medal from Shantilal Shah Government Engineering College and IPCL, and was nominated for a best-paper award by the International Association of Engineers (IAENG). The lesson wasn't "I'm brilliant." It was that the gap between an idea and a published result is mostly just the willingness to actually finish. pages.b: GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS & SOC 2 Explained | Krunalkumar Shah Security Security compliance, explained: GDPR, HIPAA, PCI DSS, SOC 2, and more The alphabet soup of compliance hides one clarifying distinction: some of these frameworks are laws, one is a contract you already signed, some are certifiable standards, and one is an auditor's attestation. Sort the seven that way — with the requirements that matter in practice — and it becomes obvious which are obligations, which are choices, and which are actually yours. Published 10 August 2026 · 12 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Compliance is trust made auditable Every security consulting conversation I have eventually lands on the same question. Not "how do we stop attackers" — that one comes with the territory — but some version of: "GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2, ISO-something… which of these actually apply to us?" It comes from founders, engineering leads, and operations people holding a 300-question vendor questionnaire — always in the same slightly exhausted tone. It's a fair question, because the alphabet soup hides a real distinction: these frameworks are not the same kind of thing. Some are laws, with regulators and fines behind them. One is a contract you accepted the day you started taking card payments. Some are voluntary standards you can certify against, and one is an accountant's opinion about you. Mix those categories up and you get the classic failure mode I keep meeting: a company proudly chasing a certificate it doesn't need while ignoring a law that already applies to it. Here is the framing that unlocks all of it: compliance is trust made auditable. Every framework below turns "trust us with your data" into something a third party can verify. And every one of them is a floor, not a ceiling — the minimum a regulator, bank, or customer will accept, not a level attackers find inconvenient. The attack families I mapped in the previous post do not check your certification status before firing. The lay of the land: seven frameworks in one table Before the deep dives, orientation. Published 15 June 2026 · 4 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Why most feedback does nothing "Good job." "This could be better." "I didn't love it." These feel like feedback, but they change nothing, because the person receiving them has no idea what to actually do differently. Vague praise is pleasant and useless. Vague criticism is unpleasant and useless. Both fail for the same reason: they describe a feeling instead of pointing at a specific, changeable thing. Useful feedback is specific, actionable, and kind — and the order matters. Specific so the person knows exactly what you mean. Actionable so they know what to do next. Kind so they can actually hear it instead of bracing against it. Miss any one of those and the feedback simply gets ignored, no matter how right you were. A simple structure I keep coming back to When I give feedback, I try to hit three beats in order. It stops me from being vague and keeps the conversation forward-looking: Observation — the specific thing I noticed, stated as a fact, not a judgment. "This function does four different things" rather than "this is messy." Impact — why it matters. "That makes it hard to test, and harder for the next person to change safely." Path forward — a concrete next step, ideally as a question. "What if each responsibility became its own small function — how would you split it?" The order matters. Lead with the observation so it's grounded, explain the impact so it's motivated, and end on the path forward so the person leaves with momentum instead of a wound. Observation grounds it, impact motivates it, and the path forward turns criticism into a next step. Praise deserves the same rigor We obsess over how to deliver criticism and get lazy with praise — but "great work" is just as empty as "needs work." If someone did something really well, tell them exactly what, so they can do it again on purpose. "The way you named these variables made the whole thing readable in one pass" teaches a repeatable skill. "Nice" teaches nothing. Published 10 August 2026 · 13 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah The three promises every attack breaks Security has a reputation for being endless — new attack names every week, each sounding like its own specialty. But underneath the naming noise, every attack is trying to break one of exactly three promises. Security professionals call them the CIA triad : Confidentiality — only the right people can see the data. Broken when secrets leak: stolen customer records, read email, exposed credentials. Integrity — the data and the system are what they claim to be. Broken when something is altered: a tampered invoice, a poisoned software update, a defaced site. Availability — the system works when legitimate users need it. Broken when service stops: a flooded server, an encrypted disk, a frozen machine. This lens is the whole trick. Ask "which promise does this attack break?" and an unfamiliar attack stops being scary vocabulary and becomes a variation of something you already understand. Ransomware is primarily an availability attack that uses malware. Phishing is usually a confidentiality attack that goes through a person instead of a computer. My own research subject — the humble fork bomb — is a pure availability attack made of nothing but permitted actions. Attackers don't respect category boundaries, and real incidents chain several types together. pages.b: What Is a Fork Bomb in Linux? | Krunalkumar Shah Linux security What is a fork bomb, and why can it freeze a Linux system? One short line of Bash can bring a healthy Linux machine to its knees — no exploit, no special privileges, nothing that looks like an attack. This is how it works, why the usual defenses aren't enough, and the approach I proposed in my research to handle it more gracefully. Published 27 May 2026 · 5 min read · by Krunalkumar Shah Run it yourself, safely. There is a real Linux machine on this site that boots inside your browser with a hard 64 MB ceiling. A fork bomb in there does exactly what this article describes and costs you nothing but a reboot. One catch worth knowing: that shell is BusyBox ash , which rejects the famous :(){ :|:& };: with bad function name — use f(){ f|f& };f instead. Same bomb, one character of difference. Open the Linux terminal The one-liner that does the damage The classic Bash fork bomb is famous for how little it takes: Warning — do not run this. Pasting this into a shell will freeze your machine almost instantly, even inside many VMs, and you'll need a hard reboot. Read on to understand it instead. :(){ :|:& };: It defines a function called : that calls itself twice and pipes one copy into the other, running both in the background — then invokes it. Each process immediately creates two more, which each create two more, and so on. There is no upper limit written anywhere. It is exponential growth with no brake pedal. The unsettling part isn't the cleverness of the code. It's that every individual action it takes is completely legitimate. Creating a process is something any user is allowed to do. Why "just one more process" ends the system Every running program on Linux is a process, and the kernel tracks each one in a finite structure called the process table. Processes also consume memory and CPU scheduling slots. A fork bomb doesn't break any single one of these — it exhausts all of them at once. The process table fills, memory runs out, and the scheduler is so busy juggling a flood of near-identical processes that legitimate work never gets a turn. The result is a machine that hasn't crashed and hasn't been hacked in any traditional sense — it is simply too busy multiplying to respond to you. In security terms, this is an attack on availability , one of the three pillars of information security alongside confidentiality and integrity. The problem is that they combine: screen, time zone, language, GPU, core count and font rendering together are usually enough to pick one browser out of millions, and none of it is stored in a cookie you can clear. Research remains central to my work, whether it is publishing academic material or applying fresh thinking to cybersecurity and practical systems. Publication Security Against Fork Bomb Attack in Linux Based Systems Krunalkumar D. Shah & Krunal V. Patel · International Journal of Research in Advent Technology (IJRAT), Vol. 7, No. 4, April 2019 · E-ISSN 2321-9637 · DOI: 10.32622/ijrat.74201911 🏅 Nominated for the Best Paper Award in Linux research at IAENG The problem I set out to solve A fork bomb is a denial-of-service attack in which a process endlessly replicates itself until the process table and memory are exhausted, freezing the system. What drew me to it is that creating a process is a legitimate operation needing no special privileges, so even hardened Linux systems are vulnerable — availability, one of the three pillars of information security, breaks down. Why the existing defenses weren’t enough Static process limits reject legitimate work once the cap is hit. Rate limits misfire on fork-heavy software such as CAD tools. Name-based blacklists never forgive: a legitimate process that shares a name with a past offender is killed forever. Each approach trades one failure mode for another, and that is the gap I set out to close. The defense I proposed I combined name-based detection with something I call process resource quarantine. New processes are monitored for their fork rate; offenders are killed and their name recorded. When a recorded name reappears, I do not kill it outright — it runs inside a resource quarantine and is inspected. If it behaves, it is released and removed from the list, so a false positive corrects itself instead of lasting forever. What my results showed I evaluated the system with a bash fork bomb on Xubuntu 18.04 (kernel 4.15). It identified an attack in as little as 44 ms at a threshold of 500 forks, while known offenders were handled instantly by name — and the machine stayed responsive and available throughout, which was the whole point. How each fork request is screened — trusted names skip checks, unknown processes are rate-checked, and repeat offenders get quarantined instead of being permanently banned. See it happen.
